items.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents for her first prenatal visit with a certain last menstrual period giving 8 weeks 4 days. Crown-rump length measures 7 weeks 5 days. How should the estimated due date be assigned?
options: Keep the last menstrual period date because the patient is certain of it
Average the two estimates and assign the due date at the midpoint of them
Use the ultrasound date, because the difference exceeds 5 days at this age
Repeat the ultrasound in 2 weeks before assigning any final date
items.explanation: At 8 weeks 6 days or earlier, ACOG advises redating when the ultrasound estimate differs from menstrual dating by more than 5 days. Here the difference is 6 days, so the ultrasound date becomes the final due date even though the last menstrual period was certain. Averaging has no basis, and waiting for a repeat scan is unnecessary because first-trimester crown-rump length is the most accurate dating method.

items.stem: A 17-year-old has primary amenorrhea and absent breast development. She is 168 cm tall, has a normal female phenotype, and pelvic imaging shows a small uterus. FSH is elevated and the karyotype is 46,XY. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Observation with annual examinations
Induction of puberty with testosterone
Vaginal dilation only, with no surgery
Bilateral gonadectomy
items.explanation: This is Swyer syndrome, 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads, a uterus, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. The retained gonads carry a high risk of gonadoblastoma and germ cell tumor, so gonadectomy is recommended at diagnosis, followed by estrogen and progestin therapy. Observation leaves the cancer risk, testosterone is not the correct hormone, and dilation addresses neither the tumor risk nor the hormone deficiency.

items.stem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at term undergoes clinical pelvic assessment. The forepelvis is narrow, the inlet is heart shaped, the sidewalls converge, and the ischial spines are prominent. Which pelvic type does this describe?
options: Android
Gynecoid
Anthropoid
Platypelloid
items.explanation: The android pelvis has a wedge or heart-shaped inlet, a narrow forepelvis, convergent sidewalls, and prominent spines, and it is associated with deep transverse arrest and difficult descent. The gynecoid pelvis is round and the most favorable for vaginal birth. The anthropoid pelvis is oval with a long anteroposterior diameter, and the platypelloid pelvis is flattened with a short anteroposterior diameter and wide transverse diameter.

items.stem: A 47-year-old average-risk woman with no symptoms has never been screened for colorectal cancer. What is the best recommendation?
options: Begin screening at age 50
Begin screening now, such as colonoscopy every 10 years or annual stool testing
Screen only if a first-degree relative has had colon cancer or polyps
Obtain a single sigmoidoscopy and then plan no further testing
items.explanation: Colorectal cancer screening for average-risk adults is recommended from age 45 to 75, using options such as colonoscopy every 10 years or annual stool-based testing. Waiting until 50 reflects older guidance, and limiting screening to women with family history misses average-risk disease. A single sigmoidoscopy without follow-up does not meet an established screening schedule and would leave her without ongoing surveillance.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a 12-week-size fibroid uterus and heavy bleeding unresponsive to medication requests hysterectomy. She has had two vaginal births and no prior abdominal surgery. Which route is generally preferred?
options: Total abdominal hysterectomy as the standard route
Supracervical hysterectomy through a midline incision
Robotic hysterectomy as the preferred route in all cases
Vaginal if feasible, otherwise laparoscopic
items.explanation: ACOG recommends vaginal hysterectomy when feasible, since it has the lowest morbidity, shortest recovery, and lowest cost, with laparoscopic hysterectomy as the next choice. An abdominal approach is reserved for very large uteri or limited access. Supracervical hysterectomy leaves the cervix and is not a default, and robotic surgery adds cost without clear benefit over standard laparoscopy for benign disease.

items.stem: A 27-year-old Rh(D)-negative woman at 28 weeks has a negative antibody screen. Her partner is Rh(D)-positive. She has had no bleeding. What is the best management?
options: Give anti-D immune globulin now and again after an Rh(D)-positive birth
Give it only after delivery, and only if the newborn is Rh(D)-positive
Repeat antibody titers monthly and treat only if a titer appears
Give no treatment now because the antibody screen is negative
items.explanation: A negative antibody screen means she is not yet sensitized, which is exactly when prophylaxis works. A 300 microgram dose of anti-D immune globulin at 28 weeks prevents sensitization from silent fetomaternal hemorrhage, and a second dose follows delivery of an Rh(D)-positive infant. Postpartum-only dosing misses antenatal sensitization, and waiting for a titer to appear means sensitization has already occurred and cannot be reversed.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had no menses for 8 months after a curettage for retained placenta following a postpartum hemorrhage. FSH and TSH are normal. She has no withdrawal bleeding after estrogen and progestin. What is the most likely cause?
options: Primary ovarian insufficiency
Intrauterine adhesions
Pituitary necrosis from Sheehan syndrome
Cervical stenosis alone with a normal endometrium
items.explanation: Curettage after pregnancy can damage the basalis layer and cause intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome). Hormone levels are normal, but the endometrium cannot respond, so no withdrawal bleeding occurs after estrogen and progestin. Ovarian insufficiency would show a high FSH, and Sheehan syndrome causes low gonadotropins with hypoestrogenism, though withdrawal bleeding would usually occur after estrogen priming. Hysteroscopy confirms the diagnosis and permits lysis.

items.stem: A newborn has ambiguous genitalia with a phallus and fused labioscrotal folds, no palpable gonads, a 46,XX karyotype, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia on day 6. A markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is found. Which enzyme is deficient?
options: 11 beta-hydroxylase
17 alpha-hydroxylase
21-hydroxylase
3 beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
items.explanation: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency blocks cortisol and aldosterone synthesis and shunts precursors, including 17-hydroxyprogesterone, into androgens, virilizing a 46,XX fetus and causing salt wasting. Deficiency of 11 beta-hydroxylase also virilizes but causes hypertension from deoxycorticosterone excess. Deficiency of 17 alpha-hydroxylase causes hypertension and undervirilization, and 3 beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency mildly virilizes girls but does not produce a markedly high 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has never received the HPV vaccine. She is not pregnant and has had normal cervical cytology. What is the most appropriate counseling?
options: Vaccination is contraindicated in any woman after the age of 26
Vaccinate only after she has had a negative HPV test
A single dose is sufficient for a woman of her age
She may receive a three-dose series after shared decision making
items.explanation: Routine HPV vaccination is recommended through age 26, and adults aged 27 to 45 may be vaccinated based on shared clinical decision making, since benefit is smaller if prior exposure has occurred. Starting at age 15 or later requires a three-dose schedule. HPV testing is not required before vaccination, and a single dose is not recommended for adults of this age.

items.stem: During a total laparoscopic hysterectomy, a surgeon controls bleeding near the uterine vessels with repeated bipolar cautery close to the pelvic sidewall and suspects ureteral injury. What is the best intraoperative evaluation?
options: Cystoscopy to confirm efflux from both ureteral orifices
Observation of urine output alone
Postoperative day 1 creatinine only
Retrograde cystogram
items.explanation: The ureter is most vulnerable where it passes beneath the uterine artery, and cautery nearby can cause thermal injury. Intraoperative cystoscopy, with intravenous dye such as fluorescein if needed, directly confirms ureteral efflux and permits immediate repair. Urine output is unreliable with one functioning ureter, creatinine may stay normal with unilateral obstruction, and a cystogram evaluates the bladder rather than the ureters.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman who is planning pregnancy had a previous child with open spina bifida. She takes no medications. Which folic acid regimen is recommended?
options: 0.4 mg daily starting after a positive pregnancy test
4 mg daily starting at least one month before conception
1 mg daily during the second trimester only
0.8 mg daily until 12 weeks of gestation
items.explanation: A prior pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect raises recurrence risk, and the recommended dose is 4 mg of folic acid daily, beginning at least one month before conception and continuing through the first trimester. The standard 0.4 mg dose is for average-risk women and should start before conception rather than after a positive test. Second-trimester supplementation is too late because the neural tube closes by about 6 weeks.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, and a body mass index of 33 wants to conceive. Thyroid function and prolactin are normal. What is the first-line medication for ovulation induction?
options: Clomiphene citrate
Metformin alone
Gonadotropin injections
Letrozole
items.explanation: Letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, has higher live birth rates than clomiphene in women with polycystic ovary syndrome and is now preferred first line, along with lifestyle modification. Clomiphene remains an alternative. Metformin alone is less effective for ovulation and improves metabolic parameters. Gonadotropins are second-line therapy because of higher cost, multiple pregnancy risk, and the need for intensive monitoring.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl asks for contraception at a visit and requests that her parents not be told. She understands the risks and benefits, and there is no sign of abuse or coercion. What is the best approach?
options: Defer prescribing until a parent gives written consent for both the visit and the method
Notify her parents of the request because she is a minor and cannot decide alone
Counsel her confidentially, provide the method, and encourage parental involvement
Refer her to the ethics committee for formal review before any prescription is written
items.explanation: Adolescents can generally consent to confidential contraceptive care, and confidentiality increases the chance they seek care and use effective methods. The physician should encourage communication with a trusted adult while respecting her autonomy. Requiring parental consent or notification deters care and violates confidentiality, and an ethics committee referral is unnecessary for a capable patient seeking a standard service. Safety concerns such as abuse would change the plan, but none exist here.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has mucopurulent cervicitis. Nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for both Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Which regimen is recommended?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once plus doxycycline for 7 days
Azithromycin 1 g orally once
Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once
Cefixime 800 mg orally once plus azithromycin 1 g orally once
items.explanation: Current CDC guidance for uncomplicated gonorrhea is a single dose of ceftriaxone, and when chlamydia is not excluded, doxycycline is added for 7 days. Azithromycin alone no longer treats gonorrhea reliably because of resistance, and ceftriaxone alone leaves chlamydia untreated. Oral cefixime is an alternative only when ceftriaxone is unavailable, and doxycycline is preferred over azithromycin for chlamydia.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman weighing 128 kg is scheduled for hysterectomy for benign disease. She has no drug allergies. Which antibiotic prophylaxis is appropriate?
options: Cefazolin 1 g intravenously given at the time of skin closure
Cefazolin 3 g intravenously within 60 minutes before the incision
Vancomycin 1 g intravenously as routine first-line prophylaxis
Ampicillin 2 g intravenously on the evening before the surgery
items.explanation: A first-generation cephalosporin is the standard prophylaxis for hysterectomy, and patients weighing 120 kg or more need a 3 g dose, given within 60 minutes before the incision so tissue levels are adequate when contamination occurs. Giving it at closure is too late. Vancomycin is for beta-lactam allergy or MRSA concerns, and ampicillin the night before leaves no coverage during surgery.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation has not received any vaccines this pregnancy. Her last tetanus booster was 5 years ago. Which vaccine should she receive today?
options: Tdap after delivery, since she had a booster within 10 years
Tetanus and diphtheria toxoids alone, without a pertussis component
Tdap, because it is given in every pregnancy
Measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine
items.explanation: Tdap is recommended during every pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks, regardless of prior booster timing, so maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn from pertussis. Postpartum dosing does not provide infant protection early enough, and tetanus-diphtheria alone omits the pertussis component. Measles, mumps, and rubella is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with amenorrhea and galactorrhea who wants pregnancy has a prolactin of 85 ng/mL. Pregnancy test and TSH are normal. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a 6 mm pituitary microadenoma. What is the best treatment?
options: Transsphenoidal surgical resection
Cabergoline
Pituitary radiation therapy
Levothyroxine replacement
items.explanation: A prolactin-secreting microadenoma responds well to a dopamine agonist, and cabergoline normalizes prolactin and restores ovulation in most women. Surgery is reserved for resistance to medical therapy or intolerance, and radiation is used rarely. Levothyroxine would help only if hypothyroidism caused the elevated prolactin, but her TSH is normal. Therapy is typically stopped once pregnancy is established, with monitoring for symptoms.

items.stem: On postoperative day 2 after an uncomplicated cesarean birth, an abdominal film obtained for pain shows a retained surgical sponge. The patient is stable and unaware. What is the most appropriate next step regarding communication?
options: Wait until the sponge is removed, then mention it only if she asks about the film
Disclose only if she later develops symptoms, fever, or evidence of infection or obstruction
Disclose promptly to her, apologize, explain the correction plan, and file a safety report
Ask the risk manager to tell her instead so that the physician avoids personal liability
items.explanation: Honest, timely disclosure of an error is an ethical duty and is supported by professional guidance. The physician should explain what happened, apologize, describe the corrective plan, and report the event through the safety system so that processes can be improved. Delaying disclosure, disclosing only if harm appears, or delegating the conversation entirely undermines trust and the patient's ability to participate in decisions about her own care.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman whose male partner is HIV-positive with a detectable viral load asks about preexposure prophylaxis. Which statement about starting it is correct?
options: She must have a CD4 count above 500 cells per cubic millimeter first
She must wait until her partner's viral load has become suppressed
She needs a negative hepatitis C antibody test and a normal liver panel first
She needs a negative HIV test and adequate renal function
items.explanation: Daily tenofovir with emtricitabine is indicated for people at substantial risk, and before prescribing, HIV infection must be excluded with an antigen and antibody test and renal function checked, because tenofovir requires adequate clearance. A CD4 count is relevant only in HIV-positive people. A partner's detectable viral load is a reason to start, not wait, and hepatitis C testing is part of routine care but is not a prerequisite.

items.stem: During operative hysteroscopy for a large submucosal fibroid using a nonelectrolyte distending medium, a patient develops confusion and seizure. Sodium is 118 mEq/L and the fluid deficit is 2,500 mL. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hyponatremia from absorption of hypotonic distending fluid
Air embolism from the uterine cavity
Hypoglycemia from sorbitol metabolism
Anaphylaxis to the distending medium
items.explanation: Glycine and sorbitol are hypotonic, and excessive intravasation causes dilutional hyponatremia with confusion, seizures, and cerebral edema. The procedure should be stopped once a fluid deficit threshold is reached, about 1,000 mL for nonelectrolyte media. Air embolism would present with sudden hypoxia and hypotension, and sorbitol does not produce clinically important hypoglycemia. Anaphylaxis would cause bronchospasm and hypotension.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman at 12 weeks of gestation has a cell-free DNA screen reporting high risk for trisomy 21. Ultrasound shows a nuchal translucency of 3.8 mm. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat cell-free DNA testing in two weeks to confirm
Obtain a quad screen later in pregnancy to confirm the result
Offer chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis
Counsel about pregnancy termination now without any further testing
items.explanation: Cell-free DNA is a screening test, not a diagnosis, and positive results should be confirmed by karyotype or microarray from chorionic villi or amniotic fluid before irreversible decisions are made. An enlarged nuchal translucency further supports offering diagnostic testing. Repeating cell-free DNA or adding serum screening only adds uncertainty, and counseling toward termination without confirmation is premature.

items.stem: A 52-year-old obese woman has had 6 months of irregular heavy bleeding. A pregnancy test is negative. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Endometrial sampling
Repeat evaluation after three more cycles of observation
Tranexamic acid with no further testing
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging as the first test
items.explanation: Women aged 45 or older with abnormal uterine bleeding, and younger women with risk factors such as obesity or unopposed estrogen, need endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia or carcinoma. Medical management is reasonable only after malignancy is excluded. Observation delays diagnosis, and imaging cannot replace histology because ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging do not reliably distinguish benign from malignant endometrium.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles asks what triggers ovulation. Which physiologic event produces the midcycle luteinizing hormone surge?
options: Falling progesterone at the end of the luteal phase releases the pituitary from inhibition
Sustained high estradiol creates positive feedback on the pituitary
Rising inhibin A from the corpus luteum stimulates gonadotroph LH release
Declining FSH from androgen feedback permits the dominant follicle to release its oocyte
items.explanation: Estradiol that stays high for roughly two days, produced by the maturing dominant follicle, reverses its usual negative feedback and drives the LH surge, with ovulation about 10 to 12 hours after the peak. Falling progesterone belongs to the late luteal phase and permits the FSH rise for the next cycle. Inhibin A is a luteal product that suppresses FSH. Androgens do not trigger the surge.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman has a femoral neck T-score of minus 2.7 on dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and no prior fracture. Creatinine clearance is normal. Which initial therapy is most appropriate?
options: Teriparatide as first-line therapy
Systemic estrogen for osteoporosis alone
Salmon calcitonin nasal spray
Oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D
items.explanation: A T-score of minus 2.5 or lower defines osteoporosis, and oral bisphosphonates such as alendronate are first-line therapy because they reduce vertebral and hip fractures at low cost, along with adequate calcium and vitamin D. Teriparatide is reserved for very high fracture risk. Systemic estrogen is not recommended solely for bone protection in older women, and calcitonin has weak fracture evidence.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman is on postoperative day 6 after a vaginal hysterectomy. After straining, she reports a sudden gush of fluid and a pelvic pressure sensation. Examination shows a loop of bowel at the introitus. What is the best immediate management?
options: Cover the bowel with moist saline dressings, keep her fasting, and go to the operating room
Push the bowel back in and discharge her with careful return instructions
Apply a vaginal pessary to support the cuff and observe her in clinic
Start oral antibiotics and reexamine her in the office in one week
items.explanation: Evisceration through a dehisced vaginal cuff is a surgical emergency. The exposed bowel should be protected with warm, moist saline dressings, the patient kept fasting with intravenous access and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and she should go promptly to the operating room for assessment of bowel viability and cuff repair. Reducing it at the bedside, using a pessary, or delaying management risks bowel ischemia, peritonitis, and sepsis.

items.stem: A 25-year-old at 32 weeks has spontaneous rupture of membranes confirmed by pooling and positive nitrazine testing. She has no contractions, fever, or vaginal bleeding, and the fetal heart tracing is reassuring. Which management is best?
options: Induce labor with oxytocin without delay
Give tocolytics for 7 days, then discharge her home
Admit, give latency antibiotics and corticosteroids, and observe
Perform an emergency cerclage to restore membrane integrity
items.explanation: Before 34 weeks without infection, abruption, or fetal compromise, expectant inpatient management prolongs pregnancy and improves neonatal outcomes. Latency antibiotics extend the interval to delivery, and corticosteroids reduce respiratory morbidity. Immediate induction would cause avoidable prematurity, tocolysis offers no benefit after rupture and outpatient care raises infection risk, and cerclage is not a treatment for ruptured membranes.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl has had heavy menses since menarche, requiring a pad change hourly, and frequent nosebleeds. Her mother has heavy periods. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Anovulatory bleeding from an immature axis
Immune thrombocytopenia
Factor V Leiden mutation
Von Willebrand disease
items.explanation: Heavy bleeding from menarche with mucosal bleeding such as epistaxis and a family history suggests an inherited bleeding disorder, and von Willebrand disease is the most common. Immature-axis anovulation is common but does not explain epistaxis or a family pattern. Immune thrombocytopenia would show a low platelet count, and factor V Leiden causes thrombosis, not bleeding. A von Willebrand panel with platelet count and coagulation studies should be sent before treatment.

items.stem: A healthy woman at 30 weeks of gestation has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.44, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 20 mEq/L. Which best explains these values?
options: Early pulmonary embolism causing hypoxic hyperventilation without renal compensation
Progesterone-driven hyperventilation with compensatory renal bicarbonate excretion
Compensated metabolic acidosis from ketone accumulation in late pregnancy
Reduced tidal volume with carbon dioxide retention from diaphragm elevation
items.explanation: Progesterone raises the respiratory drive, so tidal volume and minute ventilation increase and PaCO2 falls to about 27 to 32 mm Hg. The kidneys excrete bicarbonate to keep pH near normal, leaving a bicarbonate of about 18 to 21. This is a normal compensated respiratory alkalosis. The diaphragm rises but chest wall expansion compensates, so carbon dioxide is not retained. Ketoacidosis and embolism would not give a normal pH with these findings.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has marked irritability, depressed mood, and bloating only in the week before menses, resolving within days of bleeding. Two months of prospective charting confirm the pattern and she meets criteria for premenstrual dysphoric disorder. What is the first-line medication?
options: Oral progesterone during the luteal phase
Bupropion taken throughout the cycle
An SSRI, taken daily or only in the luteal phase
Hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy
items.explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line for premenstrual dysphoric disorder and work quickly, so they can be used continuously or only in the luteal phase. Progesterone supplementation has not been shown to be more effective than placebo. Bupropion has limited evidence, and surgical menopause is reserved for severe refractory disease after medical therapy has failed.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman undergoes a four-hour vaginal procedure in the high lithotomy position. On the first postoperative day she has foot drop and numbness over the lateral lower leg and the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Common peroneal nerve, compressed at the fibular head
Femoral nerve, stretched by prolonged hip flexion
Obturator nerve, injured during pelvic dissection
Ilioinguinal nerve, entrapped in a suture
items.explanation: Prolonged lithotomy with the lateral leg pressing on a support compresses the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head, causing foot drop and sensory loss over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. Femoral neuropathy causes weak knee extension and anterior thigh numbness. Obturator injury weakens thigh adduction. Ilioinguinal entrapment produces groin pain, not foot drop.

items.stem: A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 35 weeks of gestation has blood pressure of 168/112 mm Hg on two readings 10 minutes apart, a severe headache, and proteinuria. Platelets and liver enzymes are normal. What is the best management?
options: Expectant management in hospital until 37 weeks
Magnesium sulfate, treat the severe-range pressure, and proceed to delivery
Outpatient labetalol with twice weekly testing
Induce labor with oxytocin and withhold magnesium sulfate
items.explanation: Severe-range blood pressure with headache indicates preeclampsia with severe features. At 34 weeks or later, delivery after maternal stabilization is recommended. Magnesium sulfate prevents eclampsia, and acute antihypertensive therapy within 30 to 60 minutes lowers stroke risk. Expectant care is reserved for earlier gestations, outpatient therapy is unsafe with severe features, and omitting magnesium leaves her at risk for seizure during labor and postpartum.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman with multiple submucosal and intramural leiomyomas has heavy menstrual bleeding, a 14-week-size uterus, and desires future pregnancy. Which procedure is the most appropriate?
options: Uterine artery embolization
Total abdominal hysterectomy
Endometrial ablation
Myomectomy
items.explanation: Myomectomy removes the fibroids and preserves the uterus, so it is the preferred surgical choice for symptomatic women who wish to conceive. Uterine artery embolization is not recommended when fertility is desired because of limited data and risks to ovarian reserve and placentation. Hysterectomy ends fertility, and endometrial ablation destroys the endometrium and is contraindicated for women who want pregnancy.

items.stem: A randomized trial of a new treatment finds no statistically significant difference from placebo, but it enrolled only 40 participants and the true effect may be clinically important. Which error is most likely?
options: Type I error
Type II error
Selection bias
Recall bias
items.explanation: A type II error is failing to detect a true difference, and it is most likely when sample size is small, which reduces statistical power. A type I error is a false positive finding of a difference, which a null result does not reflect. Selection bias and recall bias are design flaws unrelated to simply having too few participants to detect an effect.

items.stem: A 29-year-old transgender man has taken testosterone for 4 years and has a cervix. He has never had cervical screening. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Screening is not needed because long-term testosterone prevents cervical cancer
Screen only if he develops vaginal bleeding or spotting
Screen with cytology on the same schedule as other people with a cervix
Perform annual cytology because testosterone therapy raises his risk
items.explanation: Cervical cancer risk depends on the presence of a cervix and HPV exposure, not on gender identity or hormone use. Testosterone does not eliminate risk, and atrophic changes may make cytology harder to interpret, so using an adequately sized speculum and sometimes topical estrogen helps. He should follow the standard age-based schedule rather than screening only for symptoms or more often than recommended.

items.stem: During operative hysteroscopy with normal saline as the distending medium in a healthy 36-year-old woman, the cumulative fluid deficit reaches 2,600 mL. Which is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue, because isotonic saline cannot cause harm
Switch to glycine to finish the resection
Give hypertonic saline for presumed hyponatremia
Stop the procedure and evaluate for fluid overload
items.explanation: With isotonic saline the main danger is volume overload with pulmonary edema, not hyponatremia, and the usual limit for a healthy woman is 2,500 mL, so a deficit of 2,600 mL means the case should stop and she should be assessed for overload, with a diuretic if needed. Continuing ignores the limit, and glycine would add hypotonic risk. Hypertonic saline treats hyponatremia, which isotonic saline does not cause.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks of gestation had preeclampsia with delivery at 33 weeks in her last pregnancy. What prophylaxis should be advised?
options: Aspirin 81 mg nightly started at 12 to 28 weeks, continued until delivery
Calcium 500 mg daily alone for the entire length of the pregnancy
Aspirin 325 mg daily started now and stopped at 36 weeks
Vitamin C and vitamin E supplements taken throughout the pregnancy
items.explanation: A history of preeclampsia with preterm delivery is a high-risk factor, and low-dose aspirin started after 12 weeks and ideally before 16 weeks lowers recurrence risk. The dose is 81 mg, not the higher analgesic dose, and it continues until delivery. Calcium helps mainly where intake is low, and antioxidant vitamins C and E showed no benefit and were associated with harm in trials.

items.stem: A 44-year-old multiparous woman has heavy painful menses and a globular, tender uterus. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a thickened junctional zone of 15 mm without discrete masses. What is the diagnosis?
options: Intramural leiomyoma
Adenomyosis
Endometrial polyp
Endometrial hyperplasia
items.explanation: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium, producing a diffusely enlarged, tender uterus, heavy bleeding, and dysmenorrhea in women in their forties. A junctional zone thicker than 12 mm on magnetic resonance imaging supports it. Leiomyomas appear as discrete, well-circumscribed masses, polyps are intracavitary, and hyperplasia is a diagnosis made on endometrial histology and does not enlarge the myometrium.

items.stem: A gynecologist at a community hospital holds a moral objection to uterine evacuation. A patient at 18 weeks with ruptured membranes and chorioamnionitis becomes hypotensive and febrile and needs immediate evacuation. No other clinician is on site. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Provide the stabilizing treatment, because emergency care may not be withheld on conscience grounds
Decline and document the objection, because personal moral integrity outweighs the patient's immediate need
Delay care until the ethics committee can convene and offer its opinion on the request
Withhold the details of her condition so that her choices are not shaped by the objection
items.explanation: Conscientious objection is respected in elective settings, but an objecting physician must still give emergency care when delay threatens life or serious harm and no alternative clinician is available. Referral is appropriate only when it does not endanger the patient. Declining outright or waiting for a committee abandons a deteriorating patient. Withholding information violates informed consent, since she must understand her condition and options.

items.stem: A 54-year-old nondiabetic woman has an LDL cholesterol of 145 mg/dL and a calculated 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk of 12%. She has never taken lipid-lowering medication. What is the best recommendation?
options: Lifestyle changes alone with a repeat lipid panel in ten years
Niacin as the preferred first-line agent
A moderate-intensity statin after shared decision making
A fibrate to lower her LDL cholesterol
items.explanation: With an intermediate 10-year risk of 7.5% to 20%, a statin is recommended after a clinician-patient discussion, along with lifestyle measures. Statins reduce cardiovascular events, whereas niacin and fibrates have not shown event reduction when added or used alone for LDL. Waiting a decade ignores her current risk, and coronary calcium scoring can help if the decision is uncertain.

items.stem: A fire starts at the endotracheal tube during an upper-airway procedure under general anesthesia with high oxygen concentration. Which is the correct immediate response?
options: Increase the oxygen flow to blow out the flame
Disconnect the monitors and wait for the fire team
Pour saline over the drapes and continue the operation
Stop the gas flow, remove the tube, and extinguish the fire
items.explanation: The immediate response to an airway fire is to stop the flow of the oxidizer, remove the burning tube, and extinguish the flame, then ventilate with room air and assess the airway injury. More oxygen feeds combustion. Waiting for others delays containment. Continuing to operate while flames persist worsens the burns. Prevention relies on controlling the fire triad of oxidizer, ignition, and fuel.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G1P0 at 38 weeks has diet-controlled gestational diabetes with normal fasting and postprandial values, normal fetal growth, and normal amniotic fluid. What is the best plan for timing of delivery?
options: Induce labor at 36 weeks because she has diabetes
Perform a planned cesarean this week at 38 weeks
Await spontaneous labor, with delivery by 40 6/7 weeks
Wait for spontaneous labor and induce at 41 weeks
items.explanation: Well-controlled diet-treated gestational diabetes carries low stillbirth risk, so there is no indication for delivery before 39 weeks. Expectant management is acceptable until 40 6/7 weeks, with induction offered if labor has not begun by then. Delivery at 36 weeks or cesarean at 38 weeks is unnecessary, and waiting until 41 weeks goes past the recommended limit.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman at about 6 weeks since her last period has an hCG of 3,000 mIU/mL, no intrauterine pregnancy, and a 2.5 cm unruptured adnexal mass without cardiac activity. She is stable with normal liver and renal function and wants to preserve fertility. What is the best treatment?
options: Intramuscular methotrexate
Laparoscopic salpingectomy
Repeat hCG in one week without treatment
Dilation and curettage
items.explanation: A hemodynamically stable woman with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy, no fetal cardiac activity, hCG below about 5,000, and normal hepatic and renal function is a good candidate for methotrexate, which avoids surgery. Salpingectomy is for rupture or contraindications. Expectant care is suitable only for declining low hCG values, and curettage cannot treat a tubal ectopic pregnancy.

items.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman has a femoral neck T-score of minus 1.9. Her calculated 10-year FRAX risk is 22 percent for major osteoporotic fracture and 3.4 percent for hip fracture. She has had no fracture. Which is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Calcium and vitamin D only, because osteopenia needs no drug
An oral bisphosphonate, because treatment thresholds are met
Repeat densitometry in 10 years before any treatment
Systemic estrogen alone for fracture prevention
items.explanation: In women with osteopenia, treatment is justified when the FRAX 10-year risk reaches about 20 percent for major osteoporotic fracture or 3 percent for hip fracture, even though the T-score is above minus 2.5. Both thresholds are exceeded here, so an oral bisphosphonate is appropriate. Supplements alone are insufficient at this risk, waiting a decade ignores it, and systemic estrogen is not used primarily for bone protection.

items.stem: During hysteroscopic endometrial ablation with an electrosurgical roller ball, the surgeon feels the instrument pass through the fundus with no resistance. The patient is stable. What is the best next step?
options: Observe overnight because small perforations heal alone
Continue the ablation and complete the procedure
Perform an immediate hysterectomy
Laparoscopy to inspect the bowel and other pelvic viscera
items.explanation: A perforation made with an energy device can burn bowel, bladder, or vessels outside the uterus without immediate signs, so the abdomen must be examined laparoscopically or by laparotomy. Simple mechanical perforations with a blunt instrument can be observed, but not energy-related ones. Continuing to apply energy risks further damage. Hysterectomy is excessive without evidence of hemorrhage.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has gestational diabetes controlled with insulin. Fetal growth is normal and fasting and postprandial values are at goal. When should delivery be planned?
options: Between 37 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks
Between 39 0/7 and 39 6/7 weeks
At 41 0/7 weeks
Between 35 0/7 and 35 6/7 weeks
items.explanation: For gestational diabetes treated with medication and well controlled, ACOG recommends delivery between 39 0/7 and 39 6/7 weeks, balancing stillbirth risk against neonatal morbidity. Earlier delivery is reserved for poor control or other complications, because late preterm and early term birth increase respiratory morbidity. Waiting until 41 weeks is excessive, since even diet-controlled disease is delivered by 40 6/7 weeks at most.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has a biopsy showing CIN 2 after an abnormal screening result. She is not pregnant and wishes to preserve fertility. What is the preferred management?
options: Simple hysterectomy for definitive therapy
Repeat cotesting in 3 years as for routine screening
Repeat HPV testing alone in 5 years as for routine screening
Observation with colposcopy and cytology every 6 months
items.explanation: In women aged 21 to 24, CIN 2 has a high rate of spontaneous regression and treatment can affect later pregnancies, so observation with colposcopy and cytology at 6-month intervals is preferred. Hysterectomy is never used for CIN, and routine rescreening intervals of 3 to 5 years would leave possibly persistent high-grade disease unmonitored for far too long.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a PHQ-9 score of 17 and reports two months of low mood, poor sleep, and reduced interest in work. She is not suicidal and is not pregnant. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and refer for psychotherapy
Prescribe a daily benzodiazepine for mood and sleep
Observe without treatment for six months
Begin a tricyclic antidepressant as the first-line agent
items.explanation: A score of 15 to 19 indicates moderately severe depression, for which medication plus psychotherapy is recommended; SSRIs are first line for tolerability and safety in overdose. Benzodiazepines do not treat depression and carry dependence risk. Observation for months is appropriate only for mild symptoms. Tricyclic antidepressants are reserved for later steps because of side effects and lethality.

items.stem: During laparoscopic entry in a 34-year-old woman, sudden hypotension occurs and the abdomen is noted to distend after the primary trocar is placed. Which is the most appropriate response?
options: Remove the trocar and observe the hemodynamics
Increase the insufflation pressure to tamponade the bleeding
Leave the trocar in place, convert to laparotomy, and obtain vascular surgery help
Continue laparoscopically with suction and a second port
items.explanation: Sudden hypotension with distension after entry suggests major vascular injury to the aorta, iliac vessels, or vena cava. The trocar should be left in place to tamponade the defect while the abdomen is opened urgently and vascular expertise is summoned. Removing the trocar frees the bleeding. Higher insufflation pressure risks gas embolism and does not control hemorrhage. Laparoscopic repair delays definitive control.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 26 weeks has fever of 39.2 C, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, and pyuria. She improves with intravenous ceftriaxone and is afebrile for 48 hours. What is the best plan on discharge?
options: Finish the course, then repeat a urine culture only if symptoms return later
Stop antibiotics once she has been afebrile for 48 hours, then observe
Change to a fluoroquinolone for long-term suppression during the pregnancy
Finish the course, then give daily suppressive therapy for the pregnancy
items.explanation: Pyelonephritis recurs in up to a quarter of pregnant women, so after the treatment course, a low-dose suppressive agent such as nitrofurantoin or cephalexin is given through the remainder of the pregnancy, with surveillance cultures. Stopping early or waiting for symptoms risks relapse and preterm labor. Fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy when safer, effective alternatives exist.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with biopsy-proven lichen sclerosus uses topical clobetasol with good symptom relief. At a follow-up visit, an examination shows a new 1 cm firm, ulcerated area at the edge of the labium majus despite therapy. What is the next step?
options: Increase the clobetasol application frequency
Biopsy of the lesion
Switch to a topical estrogen cream
Reassure and review in one year
items.explanation: Lichen sclerosus carries a lifetime risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of roughly 3 to 5 percent, so any new ulcerated, raised, hyperkeratotic, or nonhealing area warrants biopsy. Intensifying steroids or changing to estrogen would delay the diagnosis of a possible cancer, and simple reassurance is unsafe. Regular long-term follow-up is part of care for every patient with this condition.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman reports irritability, mood lability, and bloating that begin about a week before each menses and resolve soon after it starts. The symptoms impair her work and relationships. How should the diagnosis be confirmed?
options: A luteal phase estradiol and progesterone level
A single retrospective history taken at this visit
Daily prospective symptom ratings for at least two cycles
A trial of a GnRH agonist to see whether symptoms stop
items.explanation: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is confirmed by prospective daily symptom ratings across at least two cycles, which show symptoms in the final week before menses that remit shortly after bleeding begins and separate it from a mood disorder with premenstrual worsening. Hormone levels are normal in the disorder, so they do not help. Retrospective recall is unreliable, and a GnRH agonist trial is a treatment for refractory cases, not a diagnostic test.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman taking levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily for hypothyroidism has a positive pregnancy test at 5 weeks. Her TSH is 6.8 mIU/L. What is the best action?
options: Increase the levothyroxine dose by 25 to 30 percent
Continue the current dose and recheck the TSH level in 12 weeks
Add liothyronine to the current levothyroxine regimen now
Decrease the dose to avoid causing fetal hyperthyroidism
items.explanation: Thyroxine requirements rise by roughly 25 to 50 percent early in pregnancy because of estrogen-driven binding globulin and placental changes, and fetal neurodevelopment depends on maternal thyroid hormone in the first trimester. Many clinicians increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed and recheck TSH every 4 weeks. Waiting leaves her undertreated, liothyronine is not recommended, and lowering the dose would worsen hypothyroidism.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a pathogenic MSH2 variant found on testing after her father developed colon cancer. She has completed childbearing. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
options: Annual CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasound screening until age 65
Offer hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy at about age 40
Tamoxifen daily as chemoprevention against endometrial cancer
A levonorgestrel intrauterine device as complete risk elimination
items.explanation: Lynch syndrome carries a lifetime endometrial cancer risk of about 40 to 60 percent with MSH2 variants and an elevated ovarian cancer risk. Because screening for either is unreliable, risk-reducing hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is offered after childbearing, around age 40. Tamoxifen increases endometrial cancer risk, and a progestin intrauterine device may lower risk but does not eliminate it.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes for a routine visit with bruises on her upper arms and appears anxious when her husband waits outside. She is hesitant to talk. What is the best response?
options: Invite her husband in to discuss the bruises together
Advise her to leave the household immediately
Ask privately about her safety, offer resources and safety planning, and document her answers
Refer her for couples counseling to improve communication
items.explanation: Intimate partner violence should be explored in private with nonjudgmental, direct questions, followed by safety planning, resource and hotline information, and careful documentation, respecting her pace and autonomy. Discussing it with the partner present can increase her danger, and couples counseling is not recommended while abuse is occurring. Pressing her to leave abruptly can raise risk, since separation is a time of heightened danger.

items.stem: A 32-year-old primigravid woman at 39 weeks of gestation is at 7 cm with ruptured membranes. Adequate contractions have been documented by an intrauterine pressure catheter for 4 hours with no cervical change. What is the correct management?
options: Cesarean birth for arrest of the active phase
Continue expectant labor management for two more hours
Perform operative vaginal delivery with forceps
Start oxytocin and reassess after one hour
items.explanation: Active phase arrest is diagnosed at 6 cm or more with ruptured membranes when there is no cervical change for 4 hours despite adequate contractions, or 6 hours with oxytocin if contractions are inadequate. Here the criteria are met, and cesarean birth is indicated. Forceps require full dilation, oxytocin is unnecessary when contractions are already adequate, and waiting longer adds no benefit.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman leaks urine only with coughing and exertion. Urinalysis is negative, postvoid residual is normal, and a cough stress test is positive. Pelvic floor therapy has failed and she wants surgery. Which procedure is best?
options: Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA injection
Sacral neuromodulation
Anterior colporrhaphy alone for stress incontinence
Midurethral sling
items.explanation: Stress urinary incontinence from urethral hypermobility or sphincter weakness is treated surgically with a midurethral sling, which has high long-term success and low morbidity. OnabotulinumtoxinA and sacral neuromodulation treat refractory urgency incontinence, not stress incontinence. Anterior colporrhaphy repairs a cystocele but has lower success for stress incontinence than a sling, so it would not address her leakage as reliably.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman presents 18 hours after a sexual assault. She is not using contraception and has no known allergies. Which of the following should be offered at this visit?
options: Prophylaxis only after cultures and tests return
Postexposure prophylaxis only if the assailant is known to be HIV positive
Emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis, and HIV postexposure prophylaxis within 72 hours
Counseling only, with treatment deferred to a one-month visit
items.explanation: Care after assault includes forensic evidence collection with consent, emergency contraception, empiric treatment for chlamydia, gonorrhea, and trichomonas, hepatitis B vaccination if not immune, and offering HIV postexposure prophylaxis, ideally started within 72 hours. Waiting for results delays time-sensitive protection. The assailant's status is usually unknown, so prophylaxis is offered on risk. Deferring everything to a later visit misses the window.

items.stem: A 29-year-old primipara has a spontaneous vaginal birth with a fourth-degree laceration that is repaired in the delivery room. Which measure is recommended at the time of repair?
options: No antibiotic, because the wound is clean
A single dose of a second-generation cephalosporin
A seven-day course of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics
A topical antibiotic ointment to the perineum only
items.explanation: A single intraoperative dose of a second-generation cephalosporin, such as cefotetan or cefoxitin, reduces perineal wound complications after repair of obstetric anal sphincter injury, and a stool softener is advised afterward. The wound is contaminated, not clean. Extended oral courses add no proven benefit, and topical ointment does not reach the deeper repaired tissue layers.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has urgency incontinence that did not improve on oxybutynin, with dry mouth, constipation, and mild cognitive impairment. Her blood pressure is well controlled. Which next medication is most appropriate?
options: Mirabegron
A higher dose of oxybutynin
Switch to another anticholinergic drug such as tolterodine
Midodrine
items.explanation: Anticholinergic bladder drugs are associated with cognitive decline in older adults and cause constipation and dry mouth, so a beta-3 agonist such as mirabegron or vibegron is preferred when they fail or are not tolerated. Blood pressure should be monitored with mirabegron. Raising the oxybutynin dose or switching to another anticholinergic repeats the same problem, and midodrine is a vasopressor with no role in bladder overactivity.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has fatigue. Her TSH is 7.8 mIU/L with a normal free thyroxine on a first test. She is not pregnant and has no goiter or antibodies tested. Which is the best next step?
options: Start levothyroxine at full replacement dose now
Order radioactive iodine uptake scanning
Begin liothyronine to relieve her fatigue
Repeat TSH with free thyroxine in 6 to 12 weeks before treating
items.explanation: An isolated elevated TSH with normal free thyroxine is subclinical hypothyroidism, and values often normalize on repeat, so confirmation after 6 to 12 weeks is advised before treatment. Therapy is considered for symptoms, positive antibodies, TSH above 10, or pregnancy planning. A full replacement dose could overtreat. Uptake scanning is for hyperthyroidism, and liothyronine is not first-line.

items.stem: A 24-year-old nulliparous woman at 41 weeks 1 day requests induction. The cervix is closed, firm, posterior, and 3 cm long with the vertex at minus 3 station. What is the best initial step?
options: Oxytocin infusion alone at a low starting dose
Amniotomy before any ripening method
Ripening with a balloon or misoprostol
Membrane sweeping repeated daily at home until labor starts
items.explanation: An unfavorable cervix, with a low Bishop score, lowers the chance of vaginal birth and prolongs induction when oxytocin is used alone. Ripening with mechanical dilation using a Foley balloon or prostaglandin such as misoprostol improves cervical readiness. Amniotomy is not feasible with a closed, high cervix, and membrane sweeping is an outpatient adjunct that does not substitute for an indicated induction method.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman has a stage III cystocele with a bulge symptom. She is not sexually active, has significant cardiac disease, and declines surgery. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Vaginal pessary fitting
Anterior colporrhaphy
Sacrocolpopexy with mesh
Observation without any treatment
items.explanation: A vaginal pessary is an effective, low-risk first-line treatment for symptomatic prolapse and suits women who are poor surgical candidates or who decline surgery. Anterior repair and sacrocolpopexy are surgical choices that she has declined and that carry anesthetic risk in cardiac disease. Observation is acceptable for asymptomatic prolapse, but she has bothersome symptoms and a nonsurgical option exists.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 34 weeks has had one prior cesarean delivery through a classical vertical uterine incision. Her pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated. When should delivery be planned?
options: Scheduled repeat cesarean at 39 0/7 weeks
Scheduled repeat cesarean at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks
Induction of labor at 40 weeks
Wait for spontaneous labor, then perform cesarean
items.explanation: A classical incision carries a higher risk of uterine rupture before or during labor, so trial of labor is not recommended and delivery is timed before labor is likely. The recommended window for scheduled cesarean is 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks, balancing neonatal maturity against rupture risk. Waiting to 39 weeks or beyond, or awaiting spontaneous labor, exposes her to the risk of rupture.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has been unable to conceive for 12 months. She wishes to assess her ovarian reserve before planning treatment. Which test is most appropriate?
options: Midluteal progesterone to document that ovulation occurred
Serum prolactin measured on cycle day 14
A late follicular phase LH value for timing intercourse
Cycle day 3 FSH with estradiol, or anti-mullerian hormone
items.explanation: Ovarian reserve is estimated by anti-mullerian hormone, an antral follicle count, or a cycle day 2 to 4 FSH with estradiol, in which a high FSH implies diminished reserve. Midluteal progesterone documents ovulation but does not measure the egg supply. Prolactin screens for anovulation from hyperprolactinemia, and LH timing identifies the surge for intercourse. Antral follicle counts on ultrasonography give complementary information.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy and a complete placenta previa on ultrasound has had no bleeding. Her cesarean birth should be scheduled for which gestational window?
options: 34 0/7 to 34 6/7 weeks
38 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks
36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks
39 0/7 to 39 6/7 weeks
items.explanation: For uncomplicated placenta previa, delivery by cesarean is planned between 36 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks, which balances the risk of life-threatening hemorrhage with onset of labor against neonatal prematurity. Later delivery increases the chance of spontaneous labor and emergent bleeding, while earlier delivery is reserved for recurrent bleeding or other complications. Vaginal birth is contraindicated when the placenta covers the internal os.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had three consecutive first-trimester losses and is not pregnant now. Parental karyotypes are normal and the cavity looks normal on saline sonography. Which test is most likely to reveal a treatable cause?
options: A full inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden
Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibody testing
Endometrial biopsy to date the luteal phase late in the cycle
A single antinuclear antibody titer with a complement level
items.explanation: Antiphospholipid antibodies are the main treatable cause of recurrent pregnancy loss, and results must be repeated at least 12 weeks apart for diagnosis; treatment is low-dose aspirin with anticoagulation. Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended in the evaluation of recurrent loss. Luteal phase dating by biopsy has no predictive value. An antinuclear titer does not diagnose antiphospholipid syndrome.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman at 38 weeks is in active labor. The tracing shows absent variability and recurrent late decelerations that persist after position change, fluid bolus, and oxygen. What is the best interpretation and plan?
options: Category I tracing; continue routine monitoring every thirty minutes
Category II tracing; reassess the fetal heart rate in four hours
Category III tracing; stop continuous monitoring and observe her
Category III; prepare for expedited delivery if it does not resolve
items.explanation: Absent baseline variability with recurrent late decelerations is a Category III tracing, associated with fetal acidemia. Intrauterine resuscitation should be started immediately, and delivery should be expedited if the pattern does not resolve. Category I is normal and Category II is indeterminate, so neither fits. Stopping monitoring would be dangerous when the fetus may be acidemic, and waiting hours risks hypoxic injury.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has severe dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and tender uterosacral nodularity on examination. Pelvic ultrasound is normal and she does not desire pregnancy now. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: NSAIDs with continuous hormonal contraception
Diagnostic laparoscopy before any therapy is started
GnRH agonist therapy as the first treatment
Total hysterectomy with oophorectomy
items.explanation: Clinical suspicion of endometriosis justifies empiric treatment with NSAIDs and hormonal suppression, such as continuous combined contraception or a progestin, without first confirming by surgery. Laparoscopy is reserved for failed therapy or diagnostic doubt. GnRH agonists are second line because of bone loss and cost. Hysterectomy is a last resort and unnecessary in a young woman who may want future fertility.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 22 weeks with a singleton pregnancy and no prior preterm birth has a transvaginal cervical length of 18 mm. What treatment is most appropriate?
options: Weekly intramuscular hydroxyprogesterone caproate injections until 36 weeks
Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly to 36 weeks
Strict bed rest in a hospital until she delivers
Emergency cerclage at 22 weeks
items.explanation: A short cervix of 25 mm or less before 24 weeks in a woman without prior preterm birth is treated with vaginal progesterone, which lowers preterm birth risk. Intramuscular hydroxyprogesterone has not been shown to help in this setting. Bed rest does not prevent preterm birth and raises thrombotic risk, and cerclage is considered for prior spontaneous preterm birth with a short cervix, not here.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at about 5 weeks has an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy and is hemodynamically stable. Which finding would make methotrexate an inappropriate choice?
options: A hCG level of 3,200 mIU/mL
An unruptured tubal mass measuring 2.8 cm
Serum creatinine of 2.0 mg/dL
A blood type that is Rh negative
items.explanation: Methotrexate is cleared by the kidney and is toxic to marrow and liver, so impaired renal function, abnormal liver tests, and cytopenias are absolute contraindications, along with rupture, instability, and breastfeeding. A hCG below about 5,000 and a mass under 3.5 cm favor success. Rh negative status requires anti-D immune globulin but does not exclude medical therapy.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a body mass index of 41 is at 12 weeks of gestation. Cell-free DNA screening returns no result because of a low fetal fraction. She asks what this means and what should happen next. Which is the best counseling?
options: Counsel that risk is raised, and offer ultrasonography and diagnostic testing
Reassure her, because a failed test means low fetal risk
Repeat the draw once and ignore a second failure
Advise termination because the test could not be completed
items.explanation: A failed cell-free DNA result is not reassuring, because a low fetal fraction is more common with aneuploidy and with higher maternal weight, so the chance of an abnormal karyotype is raised. Management is genetic counseling, detailed ultrasonography, and an offer of chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. Reading the result as low risk is wrong. A repeat draw that is ignored if it fails again delays evaluation, and termination without a diagnosis is premature.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at an estimated 7 weeks has vaginal spotting. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an intrauterine fetal pole. Which finding makes the diagnosis of early pregnancy failure?
options: Mean sac diameter of 10 mm with no yolk sac
Crown-rump length of 4 mm with no cardiac activity
An empty gestational sac with an hCG of 1,200 mIU/mL
Embryo of 7 mm or more with no cardiac activity
items.explanation: Pregnancy failure is diagnosed when the crown-rump length is 7 mm or more without cardiac activity, or when the mean sac diameter reaches 25 mm without an embryo. A 4 mm embryo without a heartbeat and a small sac without a yolk sac are suspicious but not diagnostic, and a repeat scan in a week is warranted. Discriminatory hCG values do not diagnose failure.

items.stem: At a routine 20-week anatomy scan in a 29-year-old woman with a low-risk aneuploidy screening result, an isolated echogenic intracardiac focus is seen. The remaining anatomy is normal. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure her that this isolated finding needs no testing
Offer amniocentesis for fetal karyotype in the coming week
Refer for detailed fetal echocardiography in the next week
Obtain serial growth scans every four weeks through term
items.explanation: An isolated echogenic intracardiac focus is a common normal variant, seen in a few percent of fetuses, and carries little added aneuploidy risk when screening is low risk. No further testing, echocardiography, or extra growth surveillance is indicated. Invasive testing would expose her to procedure-related loss for no benefit. Evaluation changes only if other markers or anomalies appear or the screen is high risk.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman with a pathogenic BRCA2 variant has completed childbearing and has no cancer. She asks when risk-reducing surgery should be done to lower her ovarian cancer risk. What is the best advice?
options: Annual CA-125 with ultrasonography until menopause instead of surgery
Salpingo-oophorectomy between ages 40 and 45
Bilateral salpingectomy alone, keeping the ovaries until age 60
Surgery only after an abnormal screening result appears
items.explanation: Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy is advised after childbearing is complete, at ages 35 to 40 for BRCA1 and 40 to 45 for BRCA2, because ovarian cancer risk with BRCA2 rises later and no screening method detects early disease reliably. Annual CA-125 with ultrasonography does not lower mortality. Salpingectomy alone leaves the ovaries and their risk in place, and waiting for an abnormal screen means disease may already be advanced.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 32 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, a heart rate of 110 beats per minute, and swelling of the left calf. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Which is the most appropriate first diagnostic test?
options: A D-dimer level to exclude thromboembolism
Pelvic magnetic resonance venography
Compression ultrasonography of the legs
Ventilation-perfusion scanning before any other testing
items.explanation: With signs of deep vein thrombosis, bilateral compression ultrasonography is the best first test: a positive result confirms venous thromboembolism and treatment can begin without radiation to the chest. D-dimer rises normally in pregnancy and has poor specificity here. Magnetic resonance venography is reserved for pelvic vein questions. Lung imaging is needed only if the leg study is negative and suspicion remains.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has a rapidly growing pelvic mass. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated and hCG is normal. Pathology is expected to show which tumor?
options: Dysgerminoma
Granulosa cell tumor
Mature cystic teratoma
Yolk sac tumor
items.explanation: Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumors produce alpha-fetoprotein and occur in adolescents and young women with rapid growth. Dysgerminomas are associated with lactate dehydrogenase and sometimes mildly elevated hCG. Granulosa cell tumors secrete inhibin and estrogen, causing bleeding or precocity. Mature teratomas are benign and typically have normal markers. Fertility-sparing surgery with chemotherapy gives excellent cure rates in these young patients.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a history of deep vein thrombosis and confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome takes warfarin. She is now 6 weeks pregnant by ultrasonography. What is the best change in therapy?
options: Continue warfarin through the pregnancy with weekly INR checks
Use prophylactic-dose anticoagulation alone, as for obstetric-only disease
Switch to therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation plus low-dose aspirin
Stop all anticoagulation and give low-dose aspirin alone
items.explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome with prior thrombosis requires therapeutic-dose anticoagulation in pregnancy, with low-dose aspirin added. Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy when used from about 6 to 12 weeks, so it is replaced by a parenteral agent. Prophylactic dosing is for obstetric-only antiphospholipid syndrome without thrombosis. Aspirin alone does not protect a woman with prior venous thrombosis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman reports constant clear vaginal leakage beginning two weeks after an abdominal hysterectomy. Methylene blue instilled into the bladder through a catheter stains a vaginal tampon blue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vesicovaginal fistula
Ureterovaginal fistula
Overflow incontinence
Urethral diverticulum
items.explanation: Dye placed in the bladder reaching the vagina proves a communication between the bladder and vagina. In a ureterovaginal fistula the tampon would be wet but not blue after bladder filling, becoming colored only after intravenous indigo carmine or similar dye. Overflow incontinence produces dribbling with a distended bladder. A urethral diverticulum causes dribbling after voiding and a tender anterior mass, not constant leakage.

items.stem: A 26-year-old nulliparous woman at 39 weeks of gestation is in spontaneous labor with ruptured membranes. The tracing shows a baseline of 140 beats per minute, moderate variability, and recurrent variable decelerations to 70 beats per minute lasting 45 seconds after most contractions. Maternal position change has not helped. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate cesarean delivery for a category III tracing
Amnioinfusion with isotonic saline
Oxytocin augmentation to shorten the labor
Discontinuation of the monitor in favor of intermittent auscultation
items.explanation: Recurrent variable decelerations with moderate variability make a category II tracing, usually from cord compression after the membranes rupture. When repositioning fails, amnioinfusion with isotonic saline cushions the cord and reduces the decelerations. Immediate cesarean is reserved for a category III tracing or failure to improve. Oxytocin would increase contraction frequency and worsen compression, and abandoning continuous monitoring is unsafe while the tracing remains indeterminate.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman delivers vaginally and has a laceration that extends through the anal sphincter complex and the anal mucosa. The repair is completed by an experienced operator. Which is the most appropriate postoperative plan?
options: Prolonged opioid use to keep her bowels inactive
Daily enemas to keep the rectum clear
A binding diet to avoid any bowel movement for a week
Perioperative antibiotics and a stool softener
items.explanation: This is a fourth-degree laceration, which includes the anal mucosa, and repair should be done by a trained operator. Perioperative antibiotics lower wound infection and breakdown, and stool softeners prevent straining across the repair. Opioids and binding diets cause constipation and impaction. Enemas and manipulation of the rectum can disrupt the repair, so avoiding them is standard, and follow-up with pelvic floor counseling is added.

items.stem: A 3.9 kg newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia holds the right arm adducted and internally rotated at the side, with the elbow extended and the wrist flexed. The hand grasp is normal. Which injury is most likely?
options: Lower brachial plexus injury involving C8 and T1
Upper brachial plexus injury involving C5 and C6
Fracture of the humeral shaft
Cervical spinal cord transection
items.explanation: Waiter's tip posture with preserved grasp is Erb palsy, an injury to the C5 and C6 roots from lateral traction on the neck during delivery. Klumpke palsy from C8 and T1 injury produces a weak hand and claw posture. A humeral fracture causes pain and crepitus with an asymmetric Moro response, and cord transection causes bilateral low tone, not an isolated arm posture.

items.stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman has had three culture-proven urinary tract infections in the past year. She has no hematuria, stones, or incomplete emptying. Which intervention is most likely to reduce further infections?
options: Cystoscopy and upper tract imaging as the first step
Continuous fluoroquinolone for twelve months
Vaginal estrogen therapy
Prophylactic bladder instillations every week
items.explanation: Estrogen deficiency alters the vaginal flora and urinary mucosa, and vaginal estrogen lowers recurrence in postmenopausal women with recurrent infection. Imaging and cystoscopy are for hematuria, stones, or atypical features. Long-term fluoroquinolones carry tendon, nerve, and resistance risks and are not the first choice. Weekly bladder instillations lack evidence in this setting. Hydration and behavioral measures can supplement treatment.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with chronic hypertension has uterine atony after vaginal delivery. Bleeding continues despite uterine massage and an oxytocin infusion. She has no history of asthma. Which is the most appropriate next medication?
options: Carboprost tromethamine 250 mcg intramuscularly
Methylergonovine 0.2 mg intramuscularly
Oxytocin 40 units as a rapid intravenous push
Immediate hysterectomy without further uterotonics
items.explanation: Second-line uterotonics include carboprost and misoprostol; methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension because of vasoconstriction, and carboprost is avoided in asthma. This patient has hypertension but no asthma, so carboprost fits. A rapid oxytocin push can cause profound hypotension. Hysterectomy is a later step after medical and balloon measures have failed. Tranexamic acid can also be given early alongside these measures.

items.stem: During a hysterectomy for severe endometriosis, the surgeon finds that the left ureter was completely transected about 2 cm above the bladder. The patient is stable. Which repair is most appropriate?
options: End-to-end ureteroureterostomy of the cut ends
A ureteral stent alone left across the transection
Percutaneous nephrostomy with no reconstruction
Ureteral reimplantation into the bladder, with a psoas hitch if needed
items.explanation: A complete transection within about 5 cm of the ureterovesical junction is repaired by ureteroneocystostomy, adding a psoas hitch or Boari flap if the ureter will not reach without tension, because the blood supply of the distal ureter is poor and an end-to-end anastomosis there often fails. End-to-end repair suits injuries of the upper and middle ureter. A stent cannot bridge a transection, and nephrostomy alone leaves the ureter disconnected.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has an uncomplicated pregnancy with monochorionic diamniotic twins and normal growth in both fetuses. When is delivery recommended if no complications develop?
options: Between 38 0/7 and 38 6/7 weeks of gestation
At 39 0/7 weeks of gestation
Between 34 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks of gestation
At or after 40 0/7 weeks, awaiting spontaneous labor
items.explanation: Uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered between 34 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks because the shared placenta carries added risk of sudden fetal loss as pregnancy advances. Uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at 38 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks. Waiting to 39 weeks or beyond exposes monochorionic twins to a rising stillbirth risk without benefit.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman six days after oocyte retrieval has marked abdominal distension, ascites, dyspnea, a hematocrit of 52%, and oliguria. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Fluid restriction with a loop diuretic to reduce ascites
Home bed rest without laboratory monitoring
Emergency laparotomy with ovarian cystectomy
Hospitalization with intravenous crystalloid, thromboprophylaxis, and paracentesis if respiratory compromise persists
items.explanation: This is severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, with vascular leak causing third spacing, hemoconcentration, and thrombosis risk. Treatment is supportive in hospital with fluid resuscitation, thromboprophylaxis, monitoring of electrolytes and urine output, and paracentesis for tense ascites or respiratory distress. Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion. Surgery is reserved for torsion or rupture. Freeze-all strategies reduce the risk in later cycles.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G3P1 woman had a spontaneous birth at 28 weeks in her last pregnancy and has had no cerclage so far. At a 20-week scan, her singleton pregnancy has a cervical length of 18 mm with closed internal os and intact membranes. She has no contractions or bleeding. What is the best management?
options: Offer ultrasound-indicated cerclage placement
Strict bed rest with pelvic rest at home
Vaginal progesterone as the only intervention
Tocolysis with indomethacin for the shortened cervix
items.explanation: A prior spontaneous birth before 34 weeks plus a cervical length under 25 mm before 24 weeks is the indication for ultrasound-indicated cerclage. Bed rest and pelvic rest have no proven benefit. Progesterone alone is used for short cervix without prior preterm birth, and it adds little here once cerclage is chosen. Tocolysis treats active contractions, which she does not have.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman taking tamoxifen for breast cancer for three years reports spotting. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop tamoxifen and observe for three months
Endometrial sampling
Rely on transvaginal ultrasonography alone
Reassure her that the spotting reflects atrophy
items.explanation: Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen agonist on the endometrium and raises the risk of polyps, hyperplasia, and cancer, so any postmenopausal bleeding or spotting requires tissue evaluation. Ultrasonographic thickness is unreliable in tamoxifen users because of subepithelial changes. Stopping the drug and waiting delays diagnosis, and attributing bleeding to atrophy is unsafe before biopsy. Hysteroscopy may follow if bleeding persists after a nondiagnostic sample.

items.stem: A couple presents for counseling after both partners are found to be carriers of the same autosomal recessive condition. Their first child is unaffected and healthy. What is the probability that this unaffected child is a carrier?
options: One in two
One in four
One in three
Two in three
items.explanation: Each child of two carriers has a one in four chance of being affected, one in two of being a carrier, and one in four of being unaffected and not a carrier. Once the child is known to be unaffected, only three outcomes remain, and two of them are carriers, so the risk is two in three. One in two ignores the information that the child is unaffected.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman reports postvoid dribbling, dyspareunia, and recurrent urinary infections. Examination shows a tender anterior vaginal wall mass that expresses purulent fluid at the urethra on palpation. Which test is most useful to define the lesion?
options: Cystoscopy alone
Multichannel urodynamic testing
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis
A urine cytology study
items.explanation: These features describe a urethral diverticulum. Pelvic MRI shows the size, extent, and any complex or saddlebag configuration, and screens for rare carcinoma, guiding surgical excision. Cystoscopy may not visualize the ostium. Urodynamics assesses incontinence, not the cavity. Urine cytology evaluates urothelial cancer and would not delineate a periurethral cavity. Surgical excision is the definitive treatment for symptomatic lesions.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with peripartum cardiomyopathy had an ejection fraction of 30% that recovered to 40% eight months after delivery. She now asks about a new pregnancy. Which counseling is most appropriate?
options: Pregnancy is safe because her ejection fraction is above 30%
Another pregnancy is discouraged because of relapse and heart failure risk
Pregnancy is safe if an ACE inhibitor is continued throughout
Pregnancy is safe after twelve more months regardless of the ejection fraction
items.explanation: When ventricular function has not fully normalized after peripartum cardiomyopathy, a later pregnancy carries a high risk of recurrent heart failure, permanent decline, and death, so it is discouraged. Even with recovery to normal, relapse remains possible and needs cardiology co-management. ACE inhibitors are teratogenic in pregnancy and must be stopped. Time alone does not clear the risk when the ejection fraction remains reduced.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman and her partner have been unable to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Her cycles are regular. Which test should be ordered early in the evaluation of the couple?
options: Semen analysis
Postcoital test of cervical mucus
Testicular biopsy
Karyotype of both partners
items.explanation: Male factor contributes in roughly a third of infertile couples, so a semen analysis after a brief period without ejaculation is a first-line, inexpensive study alongside assessment of ovulation and tubal patency, and an abnormal result should be repeated. The postcoital test is no longer recommended because it does not predict pregnancy. Testicular biopsy and karyotyping are reserved for severe oligospermia or azoospermia after initial testing.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman at 8 weeks has severe vomiting and weight loss. Her TSH is suppressed and free thyroxine is mildly elevated. She has no goiter, eye findings, or prior thyroid disease. What is the best management?
options: Propylthiouracil for the first trimester
Supportive care with hydration, and no antithyroid drug
