Methimazole at a low dose
Radioactive iodine therapy
items.explanation: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis results from high human chorionic gonadotropin stimulating the thyroid in hyperemesis. There is no goiter or eye disease and it resolves by mid-pregnancy as vomiting settles, so management is supportive and expectant. Antithyroid drugs are reserved for true Graves disease. Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy because it ablates the fetal thyroid gland.

items.stem: A 29-year-old nulliparous woman at 36 weeks of gestation with a breech fetus is counseled about external cephalic version. Which finding would be a contraindication to the procedure?
options: Frank breech presentation of the fetus
Maternal body mass index of 33
Nulliparity with an unengaged presenting part
Placenta previa on a recent ultrasound scan
items.explanation: Placenta previa is an absolute contraindication to version because manipulation may precipitate hemorrhage. Other contraindications include a need for cesarean delivery for another reason, abruption, and ruptured membranes. Frank breech is the presentation most likely to be turned successfully. Nulliparity lowers the success rate but is not a contraindication, and obesity only makes the maneuver harder. Rh immune globulin is needed if she is Rh negative.

items.stem: A 35-year-old G3P2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries has a complete anterior placenta previa at 30 weeks. Ultrasonography shows loss of the retroplacental clear zone and multiple placental lacunae with bladder-wall interruption. What is the best plan for delivery?
options: Planned cesarean hysterectomy at 34 0/7 to 35 6/7 weeks, placenta left in situ
Induction of labor at 37 weeks with manual removal of the placenta
Cesarean at 39 weeks with manual removal and uterine massage
Expectant care until labor begins, with blood products on standby
items.explanation: Findings are typical of placenta accreta spectrum with a high chance of invasion. Outcomes are best with a planned cesarean hysterectomy in a center with multidisciplinary expertise and blood bank support, usually at 34 0/7 to 35 6/7 weeks, leaving the placenta undisturbed. Attempted removal causes massive hemorrhage. Waiting to term or for labor risks emergency bleeding and a worse outcome.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1 woman at 17 weeks of gestation has a maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein of 3.1 multiples of the median on quad screening. She has no medical problems. Which is the best next step?
options: Amniocentesis for fetal karyotype as the first diagnostic step
Repeat the serum screening test after an interval of four weeks
Detailed ultrasonography to confirm dating and look for defects
Plan cesarean delivery to protect a fetus with a possible defect
items.explanation: An elevated alpha-fetoprotein most often reflects wrong dating, but it also suggests open neural tube defects, abdominal wall defects, multiple gestation, or placental problems. A targeted scan answers the common causes and examines the spine and skull. Karyotyping is aimed at low, not high, values. Repeating the test or planning cesarean delivery precedes any information about the cause.

items.stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 at 34 weeks has a platelet count of 118,000 per microliter on routine laboratory testing. Her counts were normal in the first trimester, she has no bleeding, her blood pressure is normal, and liver enzymes are normal. What is the best management?
options: Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily to raise the count
Observation with repeat platelet counts
Intravenous immune globulin before delivery
Platelet transfusion before labor
items.explanation: A mild, asymptomatic fall in platelets late in pregnancy with a normal first-trimester count and no hypertension is typical gestational thrombocytopenia, which is benign and resolves after delivery. It needs surveillance only. Corticosteroids and immune globulin are reserved for immune thrombocytopenia with counts that are low or falling toward bleeding risk, and transfusion is for hemorrhage or very low counts before surgery.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with monochorionic diamniotic twins is found at 19 weeks to have an absent bladder in the smaller twin with severe oligohydramnios, and polyhydramnios around the larger twin. Which is the best management?
options: Serial amnioreduction alone as the preferred first treatment
Selective termination of the donor twin after counseling
Fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses
Immediate delivery by cesarean for fetal rescue
items.explanation: These findings indicate stage II twin-twin transfusion syndrome. Between roughly 16 and 26 weeks, fetoscopic laser ablation of the vascular anastomoses improves survival and neurologic outcome compared with amnioreduction alone, which is a lesser alternative when laser is unavailable. Selective termination is a last resort. Delivery at 19 weeks is not viable. Referral to a fetal therapy center should be prompt.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 at 22 weeks has just completed treatment for pyelonephritis with an intravenous antibiotic and has been afebrile for 48 hours. What is recommended for the remainder of the pregnancy?
options: Daily suppressive antibiotic therapy until delivery
No further therapy, if the culture is cleared
Repeat intravenous therapy every 6 weeks
Antibiotics only if she develops symptoms again
items.explanation: Pyelonephritis recurs in up to a quarter of pregnant women who do not receive prophylaxis, so after clinical improvement and completion of treatment, daily suppressive therapy, commonly nitrofurantoin or cephalexin at bedtime, is continued through pregnancy, with periodic cultures. Stopping after cure leaves her at risk of recurrence, intermittent intravenous courses are impractical, and awaiting symptoms ignores asymptomatic recurrent bacteriuria.

items.stem: A 26-year-old healthy nulliparous woman at 39 weeks is in active first-stage labor with intact membranes and no risk factors. The unit uses intermittent auscultation rather than continuous monitoring. Which schedule meets the recommended surveillance?
options: Every hour in the first stage and every 30 minutes in the second
Every 5 minutes in the first stage and continuously in the second
Every 2 hours in the first stage and every 15 minutes in the second
Every 15 to 30 minutes in the first stage, every 5 to 15 in the second
items.explanation: For low-risk women in labor, intermittent auscultation is acceptable when done at the proper frequency: every 15 to 30 minutes in the active first stage and every 5 to 15 minutes in the second stage, with the rate checked during and after a contraction. Hourly or two-hourly checks leave long gaps in which a developing abnormality goes unnoticed. Continuous monitoring is favored once risk factors appear.
